final_answer:
The zero solution is globally asymptotically stable exactly for
\[
\boxed{\{(a,b):0<a\le 1,\ b>0\}\ \cup\ \left\{(a,b):a>1,\ 0<b<\frac{\arccos(-1/a)}{\sqrt{a^2-1}}\right\}.}
\]

Here is the derivation.

The characteristic equation of
\[
\dot x(t)=-x(t)-a x(t-b)
\]
is
\[
\lambda+1+a e^{-\lambda b}=0.
\]
For a scalar linear retarded delay equation, the zero solution is globally asymptotically stable in the history sup norm iff every root of this characteristic equation has negative real part.

So we determine exactly when roots cross the imaginary axis.

Let \(\lambda=i\omega\), with \(\omega\in\mathbb R\). Then
\[
i\omega+1+a(\cos \omega b-i\sin \omega b)=0,
\]
so
\[
1+a\cos(\omega b)=0,\qquad \omega-a\sin(\omega b)=0.
\]
Thus
\[
\cos(\omega b)=-\frac1a.
\]
This has no solution if \(0<a<1\). For \(a=1\), it would require \(\cos(\omega b)=-1\), hence \(\sin(\omega b)=0\), forcing \(\omega=0\), but \(\lambda=0\) is not a root since \(1+a=2\). Hence no imaginary-axis roots occur for \(0<a\le1\). Since at \(b=0\) the characteristic equation is \(\lambda+1+a=0\), stable, the equation remains stable for all \(b>0\) when \(a\le1\).

Now assume \(a>1\). Then imaginary roots occur when
\[
\omega^2=a^2\sin^2(\omega b)=a^2-1,
\]
so
\[
\omega=\sqrt{a^2-1}.
\]
The first positive crossing occurs at
\[
\omega b=\arccos(-1/a),
\]
because this angle lies in \((\pi/2,\pi)\) and has positive sine. Therefore the first stability boundary is
\[
b=\frac{\arccos(-1/a)}{\sqrt{a^2-1}}.
\]
For \(b\) below this value all characteristic roots remain in the open left half-plane. At equality there are purely imaginary roots, so asymptotic stability fails. For larger \(b\), a conjugate pair has crossed into the right half-plane, so stability fails.

Thus the exact stability region is
\[
\boxed{
0<a\le1,\ b>0
\quad\text{or}\quad
a>1,\ 0<b<\frac{\arccos(-1/a)}{\sqrt{a^2-1}}.
}
\]
